newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: UN prosecutors seek leniency for Srebrenica killer.
newsitem.headline: UN prosecutors seek leniency for Srebrenica killer.

text.p: U.N. war crimes prosecutors said on Tuesday that a young Croat who took part in the massacre of Moslems from Srebrenica should be given a lenient sentence because he had provided valuable information about the killings.

The plea was made at hearings in the case of Drazen Erdemovic, who pleaded guilty earlier this year to taking part in the summary execution of hundreds of unarmed Moslem men after the U.N. protected "safe area" fell to Bosnian Serb forces.

Prosecutor Eric Ostberg of Sweden told the Hague-based U.N. war crimes tribunal that Erdemovic had cooperated fully with the criminal investigation into the massacre and had been the main source of information about killings in the village of Pilica.

"His role in the mass execution of innocent civilians at Pilica was significant. However, it is the view of the prosecutor that...his sentence should be substantially mitigated," documents submitted by the prosecution said.
Ostberg and U.S. prosecutor Mark Harmon said Erdemovic deserved to be treated leniently because he had been forced to commit the crime by his superiors.
Furthermore, he had voluntarily surrendered himself to the tribunal, confessed his guilt and consistently shown remorse for his role in the killings.
"His cooperation...has been invaluable and should be given considerable weight as a factor in mitigation of his sentence," documents signed by Ostberg and Harmon said.
Erdemovic, 24, appeared more at ease in the dock than in May when he wept as he pleaded guilty to crimes against humanity.
His sentence is expected early next month and will be the first handed down by the tribunal, which cannot impose the death penalty. Its maximum sentence is life imprisonment.

U.N. prosecutors allege that Bosnian Serb forces summarily executed thousands of Moslem men after seizing the eastern Bosnian town of Srebrenica in July 1995 in defiance of the United Nations which had declared it a safe haven for Moslems.
The indictment against Erdemovic says unarmed Moslem men from Srebrenica were taken in buses to a farm at Pilica near the town of Zvornik where they were shot dead by Erdemovic's unit.
"The killing of approximately 1,200 unarmed civilians during a five-hour period on July 16, 1995 was a crime of enormous proportions," Ostberg and Harmon said.
Erdemovic estimated that he had personally killed up to 100 people, they added.
Ostberg told presiding judge Claude Jorda of France that the prosecutor's office had not known of the killings at Pilica, some 70 km north of Srebrenica, before Erdemovic's confession.
Information he provided led, among other things, to a mass grave at the farm which still contained 153 bodies.

The tribunal has already charged deposed Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic with genocide over the Srebrenica massacre. Both men remain at large, in common with the majority of the 75 suspects indicted by the tribunal.
